# The Unsolved Catalogue

Compiled 17 Sept 2026 from (a) the Gallica/BnF catalogue harvest in `research/gallica_sweep/` (331 SRU records whose
descriptions mention *chiffre*; 225 items described as "avec chiffre" or "en chiffre" **without** a noted
*déchiffrement*), (b) items that S. Tomokiyo's cryptiana articles mark "undeciphered" but which do not appear on his
Unsolved Historical Ciphers list, and (c) this repo's own sweep of BnF fr. 16127. Everything below is **unvalidated
until reviewed**: entries marked ◇ were selected from catalogue descriptions only and the leaf has *not* been viewed;
entries marked ● have been viewed on the image (fr. 16127; fr. 3484 f. 34).

**Refill of 18–19 Sept 2026 (entries 34 onwards): the DECODE database.** With most of the first 33 taken to the leaf,
the catalogue was refilled from DECODE (de-crypt.org), through its JSON API with a logged-in session: all 10,106
records listed, full metadata fetched for the 1,187 ciphertext records marked *Non-decrypted* (802) or *Partially
decrypted* (385), grouped by archive series, sender, recipient and half-century, and merged where one sender wrote
from one series. Groups were dropped when they are already a target here (Sessa, Buda, Del Vasto, Gramont, Sormano,
Brèves, Moray, du Croc…) or already solved (Villeroi 1577 by Ryabov, Catherine of Aragon 1509 by the Bosbachs,
Sabran 1636 here); 27 groups in all, listed with reasons in `research/catalogue_harvest/decode/excluded.json`. The 238 entries
that remain were **scored by rule** from the metadata (a key cited in DECODE's notes or on the leaf → class A; a key
record from the same archive series → A within ten years, else B; length, language and cipher type → solvability and
difficulty; who wrote to whom and series length → importance) and are tagged *rule-scored* on the site until
reviewed by hand. Three archive-specific cautions are written into the entries: Vatican nunciature ciphers were
normally deciphered on arrival (*decifrati* filed or printed), BL Add MS 32253–32310 and TNA SP 106 intercepts were
usually deciphered at the time, and DECODE's status is sometimes stale (ACA Reserva 12 was *Non-decrypted* while its
own references cited the 1931 reading). The 1,146 ciphertext records DECODE marks *N/A* or leaves blank were fetched
but not yet sorted. Scripts and data: `research/catalogue_harvest/decode/`.

**New-solves sweep of 22 Sept 2026 (entries 272–334).** George Lasry asked for new solves and non-trivial reads
rather than letters a key already in hand reads. 63 entries were added that were nowhere in this catalogue, the
solved ledgers, TARGETS.md or any target folder, from four sources: the DECODE records marked *N/A* or left blank
(the only DECODE ciphertexts not yet referenced here), the letters Tomokiyo's cryptiana pages call "undeciphered"
while naming a cipher or key, the Gallica notices of the Nevers, Montmorency, Brèves and Rohan volumes, and the
printed calendars and recent literature. Each entry's scoring note says which kind it is: a **solve candidate** (no
key known anywhere), an **external-read candidate** (a published key, a printed decipherment or a glossed sibling in
another volume that nobody has matched to the letter), **new letters for a key held here**, or an **uncatalogued
pool**. They were scored by hand from descriptions and web checks, not from the leaves. One caution learnt on the way:
"cipher undeciphered" in Brewer's *Letters and Papers*, the HMC reports and Bergenroth usually means the editor
deciphered it himself and printed it; only "not decipherable", "sense obscure" or "no deciphering appended" mark a
letter still open (about 8 of 150 such calendar hits). The same day every new entry was checked for prior art (Tomokiyo, Lasry's GL.htm, the DECODE record, the
named calendar or edition, recent papers): seven were found already read and removed (285 Mary Stuart to Mauvissière
1584, 288 Isabella to Estrada Oct 1503, 286 Soranzo 1553, 324 Surian 1558, 315 Henri IV to Nevers 1591, 299 Beaton
and Mary Stuart's side 1575–80, 274 Clarke to Caffarelli 1812; see SOLVED_CATALOGUE.md), eight were narrowed to the part
still unread, and each remaining entry's status now states what was checked and found. Eleven entries with a partial reading by others were then removed too (listed in SOLVED_CATALOGUE.md), and
eight whose prior art could not be settled were set aside until the deciding source is reached; they can come back
under new ids:

- **“Chiffre de 13043”, a letter wholly in figures** (BnF fr. 3986 no. 32 f. 72; catalogue 272): Tomokiyo (league.htm) calls f. 72 undeciphered but links it to his Cryptologia 43(1) 2019 paper, which gives preliminary decipherments of three 1593 continuous-figure ciphertexts. The paper is paywalled, so whether f. 72 is one of the three is unconfirmed (checked 22 Sept 2026).
- **Jacomo Zambon, London, to the Council of Ten** (ASVe Capi del Consiglio dei Dieci, Lettere di ambasciatori, Busta 14 ff. 62–63, 75–76; catalogue 278): Tomokiyo describes both letters but gives no reading, and neither is in CSP Venice v. DECODE nonetheless marks R1849/R1850 'Decrypted' (Italian plaintext, no text attached), so the third image of each record needs checking for a decipherment (checked 22 Sept 2026).
- **Juan Manrique and Francisco de Toledo, Rome, to Charles V** (AGS Estado leg. 882 ff. 15–18; catalogue 289): Probably unread (22 Sept 2026): DECODE marks R9965 Decrypted, but Tomokiyo found that the attached texts belong to other dates, and CSP Spain XIII does not calendar the 9 Feb 1555 letter. The DECODE attachments need checking against ff. 15-18 before the label is corrected.
- **Sforza chancery ciphertexts, Carteggio Sforzesco boxes 1591, 1597, 1598** (Archivio di Stato di Milano, Carteggio Sforzesco cart. 1591, 1597, 1598 (DECODE R5297–R5587, 110 records); catalogue 292): Unresolved (22 Sept 2026): all 377 DECODE records from the Sforza 'Chiavi e cifrari' boxes are unclassified, and no reading was found. Because the boxes are the chancery's key series, the 169 'ciphertext' records may be key samples or exercises rather than letters, so check the images before treating them as unread correspondence.
- **Mihály Teleki's letter book** (DECODE R4819–R4834; catalogue 293): The DECODE records have no decryption and no images. The Gergely edition (1905-26), the likeliest place for a printed decipherment, was not available in full text (Arcanum paywall), so any earlier reading is unconfirmed (checked 22 Sept 2026).
- **Juan de Vega, Rome, to Prince Philip** (AGS Estado leg. 873 f. 4; catalogue 323): Tomokiyo identified the Imperial Cipher of 1544-54 but gives no reading. DECODE now marks R9964 'Decrypted' (with the author wrongly given as 'Juan de Mena') but attaches no text, so the images need checking for a marginal decipherment (checked 22 Sept 2026).
- **Adrian VI to Charles V** (Kolosova 2017, letter no. 31, p. 642 (not in Gachard 1859); catalogue 325): Probably already read (22 Sept 2026): Kolosova's 2017 thesis edits the letter (appendix no. 31, p. 642), and Tomokiyo does not flag it as lacking a decipherment. The appendix could not be reached to confirm this.
- **Uppsala E 379 G, Latin letters with digits** (Uppsala UB E 379 G (DECODE R5041–R5136, 72 records); catalogue 332): DECODE's 72 records carry no decryption text, but 53 are flagged as having inline plaintext, which suggests decipherments written on the leaves at the time. Settling it needs the Uppsala catalogue entry and the images, which require a login (checked 22 Sept 2026).

The catalogue is for letters that need cryptanalysis, not key lookups, so the 21 new entries whose key is already held
here or published (Tomokiyo, Lasry, Friedmann, Cerioni, the Nevers collection, a cifrario in the same file) were moved
out the same day to the list of letters readable with keys in hand; the key for each:

- Nevers to the Duchess, 36 figures (BnF fr. 4712 f. 10; catalogue 282): too short (36 figures) and only key trials left.
- Châteauneuf, La Marck and d'Iberville: the twelve despatches with no over-written plaintext (BL Add MS 61574 (DECODE R8052, R8054, R8068, R8070, R8075, R8078, R8080, R8081, R8086–R8088); catalogue 294): plaintext written over the cipher in 26 sibling records.
- Cardinal Gualterio and Abbé Botti (BL Add MS 20443 (DECODE R8617–R8718, 48 records); catalogue 295): Gualterio cipher tables at the BL (Add MS 20244).
- Nuncio Sega, Paris, to the Secretariat (AAV Segr. Stato Francia 32; catalogue 297): Meister and morosini1588 keys to try.
- Lope Hurtado de Mendoza, Rome, to Charles V (Jan 1521) (RAH Salazar A-20 f. 21; catalogue 301): lopehurtado key to try.
- Alonso Sánchez, Venice, to Charles V (CSP Spain iii/2 no. 468 (“no deciphering appended”); catalogue 302): Sánchez 1522 key held (sanchez1522).
- Walsingham to (probably) Dale (Folger Shakespeare Library (free images); catalogue 304): Cecil–Norris key held (norreys1567).
- Spinelly to Wolsey (Letters and Papers ii 1553 (“not deciphered”); catalogue 305): Tomokiyo 2023 Spinelly key.
- Dodieu de Vély to Montmorency (BnF fr. 20506 ff. 49, 52; catalogue 308): Tomokiyo Dodieu Cipher 1.
- Nicolas de Baugy to Mangot (BnF Clairambault 369 ff. 2, 59; catalogue 309): Tomokiyo Baugy key.
- Sancy, Constantinople, to the King and Puisieux (BnF fr. 16148 ff. 200, 206; catalogue 311): Sancy Cipher-2 from glossed pairs in the volume.
- Péricard to an unknown recipient, Paris (BnF fr. 3984 no. 73 f. 152; catalogue 313): Tomokiyo Péricard key (no. 69).
- Spanish ciphers in fr. 3641: the unread letters (nos. 27, 48, 50, 58) (BnF fr. 3641 nos. 27, 48, 50, 58; catalogue 319): Nevers key no. 54 and Cp.30.
- Dinteville and the cardinal of Ferrara: letters keyed by Friedmann (NAF 4206) (BnF Dupuy 547 ff. 97, 157, 171, 215; fr. 3020 ff. 87, 103; fr. 3126; fr. 3000 f. 74; catalogue 322): Friedmann keys (NAF 4206).
- Catherine of Aragon to Ferdinand, 29 July 1509: the cipher passage (AGS Tratados con Inglaterra L. 5 (letter of 29 July 1509; f. 60 unidentified); catalogue 326): Catherine of Aragon cipher solved (MTC3 2018).
- Charles de Gonzague-Clèves to Nevers (BnF fr. 3993 nos. 40 (f. 71), 174 (f. 254); fr. 3982 f. 51; catalogue 327): Nevers key no. 70.
- Gramont to Villandry, Rome (BnF fr. 2980 nos. 21–22, ff. 29–30; catalogue 328): Gramont 1530 key held (gramont1530).
- Cosimo I to Agnolo Niccolini (ASF (DECODE R4034–R4054); catalogue 330): cifrario R4033 in the same file.
- Nevers–Mantua letters and Badalocchio to Nevers (BnF fr. 4698 nos. 2–5, 47, 92; fr. 4700 nos. 38–46; catalogue 331): Nevers key no. 35 (gonzaga1590).

**Archive scan of 23 Sept 2026 (entries 334–348): outside DECODE.** With DECODE exhausted, five sweeps searched
archives and printed sources elsewhere, with two aims: an unread ciphertext older than the project's oldest reading
(Florence 1425), and hard targets that need a break rather than a key. Notes, dead ends and sources are in
`research/oldest/scan_2026-09-23/`. No unread ciphertext from before 1425 has images online anywhere we could reach. The Hanse
and Baltic, Hungarian, Imperial, Polish and Bohemian editions before 1450 contain no cipher letter that is not
Italian, a bare key or already edited, and the French and English ones none of any length. The four early entries
(334 Benedict XIII c. 1400, since removed: read by Puig y Puig in 1920; 335 Florence 1414, 336 Siena 1421, 337 Faenza
1425) need photographs ordered from Florence and Siena. The later ones come from HCPortal (hcportal.eu, whose historical unsolved records are
the Marburg HStAM files), Láng's 2015 inventory of Habsburg–Hungarian ciphertexts, and the TNA and Kalliope catalogues.
Items that a held or printed key reads were left out: the Marburg key-volume samples (HStAM 4 d Nr. 1219, 1220,
1224), Breuner 1583 (DECODE key R1590), the Jung-Stilling diaries (transcripts survive) and Tattenbach 1644 (broken
on Cipherbrain).

**Archive sweep of 26 Oct 2026 (entries 372–627): archives outside DECODE and Gallica.** Nine sweeps searched the
archives and letter portals not yet covered: the Torre do Tombo (DigitArq's open JSON API), the AGAD inventories in
Warsaw and the Kraków records on DECODE, the Danish Rigsarkivet and Swedish Riksarkivet, Vienna's
Archivinformationssystem, FranceArchives, Kalliope and Archivportal-D, Founders Online and EMLO, and the Medici Archive
Project; the Nationaal Archief and KHA leads of 23–25 Oct were added at the same time. Every row was checked against
this repository (catalogue, ledgers, targets, the 24 Oct Archives nationales and Riksarkivet sweeps) and the DECODE
list; 26 rows were left out as already worked, closed by an earlier sweep, or not described as cipher
(`research/archive_sweep_2026-10/exclude.json`). Per-letter rows of one writer in one volume were grouped. These entries are
scored from archive descriptions (◇) unless the sweep viewed a scan (●), and most need images ordered. Largest groups:
Stanisław August's envoys Deboli (St Petersburg) and Zabłocki (Berlin), 1780–94; Portugal's Restoration embassies in Paris
and The Hague, 1642–60; Ferdinand I's Constantinople and Ragusa ciphers, 1530–55; Maximilian I's envoys, 1510–16;
French consular and colonial letters marked "non déchiffrée"; and from a full Archivportal-D pass (entries 553–612,
through the open Deutsche Digitale Bibliothek Solr index), the Teutonic Order's cipher of Grand Master Albrecht,
1514–24, Willem Lodewijk of Nassau to his brothers, 1605–20, and fifteenth-century Saxon pieces. Blocked and to be rerun: szukajwarchiwach.gov.pl (bot
check), the Medici Archive Project (login), PARES (rate limit; Simancas covered instead from the printed Paz catalogues, entries 613–627, from Paz Catálogos II–V; the later printed volumes have no full text online; the rest of that sweep's rows, AGS Estado and AGI Estado cipher letters and intercepts 1516–1820, are entries 722–755). Method, scripts and dead ends per archive are in each
sweep's `research/<archive>/README.md`; the brief and merge are in `research/archive_sweep_2026-10/`.

**US National Archives sweep of 27 Oct 2026 (entries 628–648).** Three passes over NARA and US diplomatic sources: a
keyword sweep of the whole NARA catalogue (`research/nara_catalog/`; titles, notes and OCR text, before 1951); the State
Department's despatch series, FRUS, Manning's diplomatic correspondence and the Continental Congress papers
(`research/nara_state/`); and military, intelligence and captured records (`research/nara_military/`). The catalogue
describes most of this at series level, so the yield is small: Rose Greenhow's 1861 cipher leaves (her 1864 key is in RG
45, M1091), the Astrea packet of French consular despatches (1798–99), Cornwallis–Balfour intercepts (1780–81), coded
passages left undecoded in Manning's prints of Appleton (Cadiz 1823), Everett (Madrid 1825) and Poinsett (Chile 1813),
the French cable Sheridan's telegrapher copied in 1866, Bunch's Charleston cryptograms, the Eckert telegram ledgers, and
the 30 unbroken German Army hand-cipher messages of 1941 on the CryptoCellar list (dropped from the 14 Oct Cryptoole
import as Enigma). Not reached: Weber's *United States Diplomatic Codes and Ciphers* (1979, not online), HathiTrust
full text (bot check), item lists for RG 457 and RG 165.

**NARA full-text sweep of 27 Oct 2026 (entries 649–680).** NARA's whole catalogue, with the OCR text of every
digitised frame, is published as AWS Open Data (s3://nara-national-archives-catalog). `research/nara_reels/bulk_scan.py`
streamed the export for RG 59, 84, 45, 38, 165, 107, 393, 76, 11, 457, 65 and 360 (no catalogue API call, so no rate
limit or bot check) and flagged every frame that reads as numeric code or names a cipher (about 121,600 hits). Three
triage passes classed them by publication (`research/nara_triage_a/` to `_c/`, coverage tables in each README):
State Department numeric code runs only from 1789 to 1840, most decoded at the time; the open ones are Delacroix to
Létombe 1797, Crawford (Paris 1813–14), Anthony Morris (Cadiz 1813–15, a code no table here matches), Ellis (Mexico
1836–39) and a second Poinsett despatch. From 1906–50 the open items are German telegrams the US legations obtained
in 1917–18 (Stockholm, Lima) and a Bernstorff telegram of 11 Jan 1917. RG 457 and the military files add named
unsolved items not yet digitised (GC&CS "Unsolved Problems" 1944, the Tampico message 1917, Buenos Aires embassy
codes 1945) and one workable book code (Communist Party of America, 1920–21, M1085 roll 940). The JQA code
(`targets/jqa`) turns out to be the Department's general code of 1803–40 and reads several of these runs.

**NARA second pass (entries 681–703).** Two more detectors over the same export: five-letter code words and letter
ciphers (`bulk_scan.py --letters`, which numeric scoring misses), and every frame whose OCR names a cipher, cryptogram
or secret ink in RG 165 and RG 65 (`--words`; 4,335 frames, mostly Military Intelligence index cards and Bureau of
Investigation case files, all read). Triage in `research/nara_triage_d/` and `_e/`: Richard Taylor's Confederate
telegram books of 1864–65 copy the Vigenère words as sent (COME RETRIBUTION, COMPLETE VICTORY); the MID cards name
cipher letters and telegrams of 1917–21 that Riverbank or MI-8 could not read (the Gulick message, Hindu–German
conspiracy letters, the Black Tom network, Obregón's 1921 code telegrams) and a Revolutionary War code letter sent to
MID in 1934. Most of the files the cards cite (RG 165 entry 65) are not digitised.

**NARA sweep completed (entries 704–707).** The last record groups, RG 109 (Confederate), RG 242 (seized foreign
records) and RG 94 (Adjutant General), went through the numeric, letter-code and a polyalphabetic pass (capital-letter
runs with a low index of coincidence, for Confederate Vigenère; RG 109, 107, 393, 45). Every pass covered all 400 export
files of its record group. Triage in `research/nara_triage_f/` (no candidate: oath forms, accounts, clear telegram
books) and `_g/`: Luftwaffe Flak radio traffic of April–June 1940 in a hand double transposition (T405 roll 9; the
1939 key card on the same roll decrypts its exercise message), British and French consular cipher telegrams copied in
Spain in 1939–40, and Kriegsmarine Etappendienst telegrams in a code-plus-transposition system. RG 94 gave nothing.
Known limits: OCR finds cipher only where it is legible as print or capitals, so short cipher runs in handwritten books
are missed (the Taylor books were found by other means); the AGO Document File 1890–1917 has no OCR hits in the export;
the MID files behind the RG 165 cards and most RG 457 items are not digitised.

**NARA, the other 540 record groups (entries 708 onward).** `research/nara_reels/bulk_all.py` runs every detector at
once over the record groups not scanned above, smallest first, mass series last (Census, draft registration, pensions,
Civil Service, WPA, NARA's own RG 64), skipping personnel files. Triage in `research/nara_triage_h/` (coverage table per
record group in `coverage.md`) and `_i/`. So far: an AEF Siberia field message of 9 July 1919 in 32 five-letter groups
(M917 roll 9, not a periodic Vigenère, Beaufort or Playfair), the AEF G-2 file on enemy codes and intercepted messages
1917–18 (RG 120, not digitised), Chicherin to Sukhanov 1918 (RG 395), the Office of Censorship's secret submissions
1942–45, I.G. Farben "Duisberg" code messages (RG 131) and the U.S. Mint coded telegrams. OSS (RG 226) and the Secret
Service (RG 87) gave nothing open: the criminals' cipher letters in RG 87 were read at the time. Slice I (62 more
groups, entries 718–721) added cipher samples sent to the Chief Signal Officer 1861–69 (RG 111), two coded items in
Justice Department enemy-alien files of 1917–18 (RG 60) and a cypher letter from Leavenworth, 1916 (RG 75), each known
only from a series description or index card. The 1919 Peace Commission "undeciphered" groups (RG 256) were garbled
American cables, resent or read; the Nuremberg mentions (RG 238) point to papers not in the files.
Slice J took the three largest groups: Navy deck logs (RG 24) and census index cards (RG 29) gave nothing, and RG 64
gave entry 756, Russian Foreign Ministry cipher circulars to the New York consulate 1888–1910 (M1486 roll 83), filmed
with the instructions and examples for the bigram keys they used. Slice K scanned the export's 5,192 donated and
presidential-library collections (216,000 files) and found no unread cipher: the one real code text, Marshall's 19 June
1942 telegram to Roosevelt, has its meaning typed below it. Every file of the export has now been scanned. Slice L (`research/nara_triage_l/`) ran the two detectors the 15 earliest-scanned groups had missed (capital-letter runs and cipher vocabulary) and added 757 (a 1918 cipher cable to the US Consul-General, Auckland, that he could not read) and 758 (Coahuila state code telegrams, 1906, that the Mexican Embassy could not decipher), 759 (German, Japanese and French Legation code telegrams at La Paz 1941-42, returned by the FBI unread) and 760 (Otto Joseph's code messages, Lima 1941), and found the 1921 Constantinople intercepts of entry 669 digitised on M316 rolls 40-48 (about 390 frames); the 1938 Heeresgruppenkommando 2 Enigma messages on T311 rolls 42 and 123, set aside earlier as out of scope, were re-checked and are read at the time (clear drafts filed beside them; roll 42 published by Deavours and Kruh 1990 and decrypted by Weierud).

**US manuscript libraries (Oct 2026).** Five further US sweeps (`research/us_loc/`, `us_clements/`, `us_friedman/`, `us_beinecke_folger/`, `us_huntington/`) searched the Library of Congress (loc.gov API, 116 digital collections), the William L. Clements Library (U-M finding aids), the Marshall Foundation's Friedman Collection (Sheldon's item guide and the NSA Friedman papers), Yale's Beinecke and the Folger, and the Huntington (OAC finding aids, Digital Library, catalogue) and added 79 entries (761-839). Most are scored from catalogue descriptions only; the strongest are the Wilkinson ('Agent 13') Spanish ciphers in the LoC copies of Papeles de Cuba leg. 2374, Barras to Rochambeau 1781 'not decoded' (Beinecke), the Utah War letter of 1858 (Beinecke), the 1729 Blathwayt intelligence code (Huntington, deciphered siblings digitised), Kerlerec's 1756-57 cipher despatches (Huntington) and the 1780-81 Clinton Papers ciphers Friedman listed as undeciphered. Each folder's README lists what was not reachable (finding-aid sites that refused scripted access or served a human check; most Clements, Beinecke and Huntington items are not imaged).

**Chicago archives (Oct 2026).** Five sweeps (`research/chi_newberry/`, `chi_uchicago/`, `chi_nara/`, `chi_polish/`, `chi_riverbank/`) covered the Newberry, the University of Chicago, NARA Chicago, the Polish Museum of America and the Riverbank papers (now at NYPL, MssCol 176). 5 entries (847-851) from the first four sweeps, 3 of them tagged 'needs archive scans' (Burr's cipher letter to Wilkinson, Newberry Graff f*502; Ayer MS 1297; the Riverbank 'Mexican codes' boxes). NARA Chicago and the Polish Museum gave no entries; the Chicago trial of Gupta (Crim. 6082) is digitised and shows its cipher exhibit was read at Riverbank (catalogue 694 updated). The University of Chicago sweep read 2,024 of 2,025 finding aids and added two weak entries (852-853, both archive-only): the Harper papers' memoranda on the Sisson code messages and a 'cipher' note in the Dennis Theosophical collection. The Durrett and Wilkinson collections hold no cipher.

**UK archives (Oct 2026), batch 1.** A sweep of The National Archives' Discovery catalogue (open JSON API, about 20 cipher terms, 11,568 records, which also covers Bodleian, Lambeth and record-office entries held in Discovery) in `research/uk_tna/` gave 24 candidates; 20 are entered here (860-879), all tagged 'needs archive scans' because Discovery reports none of them digitised. The strongest are the 1723 Atterbury plot papers (SP 35/46), the 1745 Jacobite letters 'partly in undecoded cipher' (SP 36/66), Charles I's cipher letter to Ormonde, 1648 (Northumberland ZSW/554/1), and Whitworth's Moscow despatches of 1708-09 (SP 91/5-6, one undeciphered duplicate of a deciphered folio). Two Cornwallis rows (PRO 30/11) are held back because Saberton (2019) decoded the southern British ciphers; two low-weight rows follow later. Prior art beyond Discovery text, known.py and two web searches is not yet checked for these rows (printed calendars, Saberton, Lasry).

**Vatican (Oct 2026).** The Vatican sweep (`research/vat_vatican/`) could not search DigiVatLib or the Apostolic Archive (both refused scripted access), so its four entries (880-883) come from DECODE records of the Segreteria di Stato marked N/A and not yet in this repository: Francia 346 (62 records, Barberini to Ceva, 1632-34, same file as Lasry's keyed R74-R84), Francia 32 (Sega, Paris, 1590), Spagna 22 (Sega, Madrid, 1579) and Francia 173 (Ranuzzi, 1684-85, probably in print). Images were not opened, so the 'online' tag is inferred and some records may be key sheets.

**Austria (Oct 2026).** The Austrian sweep (`research/aut_hhsta/`) re-ran the State Archives' Archivinformationssystem over 22 cipher terms (665 records; 162 image-bearing records read in full; 48 dropped as 'interlinear dechiffriert') and added 12 entries (884-895) not already in `research/central_archives/`: 11 tagged online. The Türkei I and Maximiliana records are labelled 'Kein Zugang (Reservatbestand)' but their scans open without login in the AIS viewer. Strongest: the ca. 1608 Rudolf II / Matthias letters to Archduke Ferdinand (884, a page viewed, with a possible crib), the 1548 Martinuzzi/Isabella letters to Ibrahim Pasha (885, each with a Latin exemplar), and Ferdinand I's 1548-50 despatches to Malvezzi (891-893, same key family as malvezzi1548). Except for 884 the scores come from the archive descriptions, and a 'chiffriert' tag can mean one ciphered line. ÖNB holds only treatises and printed books here; Archives Portal Europe and zobodat were blocked.


Failure mode first: "avec chiffre" in Omont's inventories means the letter contains cipher, not that it was never
read. The Court's decipherment may sit in another volume, a modern edition (Scheurer's du Bellay, which prints in clear the 16 June 1529 block of item 4 that DECODE R3688 lists as
not decrypted (checked 9 Oct 2026), Mousset's Longlée,
Savasse's Maisse) may print a clear text, and Tomokiyo may already have a key that reads the leaf even where he wrote
"undeciphered". Each entry therefore lists what would confirm it is genuinely open. Coverage checks were made against
Tomokiyo's unsolved list and his French pages for Henri III, Henri IV, Nevers, Mayenne, the League and fr. 4715 (copies
in `research/gallica_sweep/src/`); his François I era article was **not** fetched (*), so 1520s–1550s entries carry that caveat.

**Internet Archive and HathiTrust sweep of 28 Oct 2026 (entries 897–1134; 238 rows).** Three passes (`research/ia_meta/`, `research/ia_fulltext/`, `research/hathitrust/`). Archive.org's own metadata almost never describes cipher content (about 2,150 hits, nearly all printed treatises, codebooks and newspapers; one manuscript, Penn Ms. Codex 88). The productive route was archive.org full text: about 330 OCR volumes of printed calendars (Letters and Papers Henry VIII, CSP Foreign/Domestic/Ireland/Scotland, the Clarendon calendar, HMC Salisbury and Heathcote) searched for editors' notes such as "cipher, undeciphered", giving 85 item-level rows (ia_fulltext), 13 (ia_meta) and 10 (hathitrust). Every row is scored from the printed note only (`seen: catalogue`); "undeciphered" in a calendar usually means no contemporary decipherment in the manuscript, and the editor may have read it, so the abstract can already hold the sense. HathiTrust itself returned a Cloudflare challenge on every endpoint and was not circumvented; its rows link the archive.org copy. Left out: 40 Commonwealth entries with no entry number or garbled OCR, and ia_meta aggregates superseded by item-level rows. Not reached in pass 1: CSP Venetian and Spanish, Cecil/Salisbury beyond Part IV, most HMC reports, Treasury Papers, Thurloe, Carte.

**Second pass, same day (130 of those rows).** Pass 2a (`research/ia_pass2_a/`, 14 rows) read about 200 more calendar volumes (Venetian, Spanish, Salisbury I–XXIV, Domestic Charles I/II); editors there print the decipherment beside the cipher, so the yield was small. Pass 2b (`ia_pass2_b/`, 22 rows) covered Stuart Papers, Thurloe, Ormonde, Treasury, Colonial, about 90 HMC reports and Burnett's Continental Congress letters. Pass 2c (`ia_pass2_c/`, 94 rows) searched non-English editions and catalogues: 45 rows from the Real Academia de la Historia's Salazar y Castro catalogue (volumes A-7 to A-14 and N-23, 1472–1513, none on DECODE), 20 from the Lope de Soria archive (BRAH 1931), 15 from the Naples Farnese inventory, and others. Same caveat as pass 1: scored from the printed note, none viewed. The Salazar rows were filtered by the absence of "descifr/traducc" in the entry, and RAH images of those volumes were not checked, so solvability is a guess. Key leads, not rows: Salazar A-15 "cifra general" (bears on `targets/garcilaso1498`), CSP Domestic James I 1611–18 nos. 121–122 (Overbury key), Salisbury XIII and XIV key tables. About 1,000 Salazar entries of 1520–29 (A-19 to A-26) are not yet itemised.

## The 1093 open targets, by priority

Scores (1–5, judgements made before viewing the leaf, data in `catalogue.json`): **importance** = what a full reading
would add to the record; **solvability** = odds of a full reading with the material online; **difficulty** = technical
work at the keyboard (1 align a known sibling, 5 statistics-only on a large nomenclator). **Priority** (0–10) blends
them with weights 0.4 / 0.35 / 0.25 on importance, solvability and ease (6 − difficulty); the site page lets you
reweight, filter and sort. Class **A** siblings with decipherment in the same volume (key recoverable by alignment, as for
Feuquières and Catinat); **B** partial key in print (Tomokiyo) or known family; **C** no key, no sibling.

II pp. 406-408 (April 1644, flagged 'In Cipher', Master of the Horse; letters of 18 and 23 Apr 1644); vol. III pp. 27-28 (Oct 1644, flagged '[In cipher]'); pp. 63-64 and 69-70 (March 1645); pp. 73-74 (Hereford, 31 Mar 1645); p. 100 (Daventry, 8 June 1645); pp. 125-128 (Digby to Legge, answering Legge's of 22 June; Legge's reply, pp. 128-131, cites Digby's letter of 30 June 1645); pp. 151-156 (Bristol, 28-29 July 1645). Staffordshire item dates from the TNA Discovery API (28 Oct 2026): /37 = 30 Apr 1644 (Master of the Horse; matches Warburton II 406-408, whose letters are dated 18 and 23 Apr, so date mismatch), /39 = 10 Oct 1644 (Warburton III 27-28), /41 = 8 Mar 1645 (III 63-64, matched on content), /45 = 31 Mar 1645 (III 73-74, exact date), /54 = 8 June 1645 (III p.100, exact), /56 = Digby 30 June 1645 (III 125-128, printed in full as plain text; the 'coded part not deciphered' is therefore deciphered in print). So six of the twelve items are printed in 1849 with plaintext. Warburton leaves Rupert's own name and some name-cipher groups as '[cipher]' or bare numbers (e.g. '92, 352' in the 29 July 1645 letter, III p.156) and says (II p.471 fn) that he gives uninterpreted ciphers only where he cannot read them. Not located in Warburton: /46 /47 /48 /49 /53 /55 (dates not retrieved) and /59 (Rupert, 9 Aug 1645, 'not deciphered'; the last printed Rupert-Legge letter is 29 July 1645). HMC Dartmouth (1887) calendars only Rupert-Legge letters of 1661. Whole reel OCR read (fetched 27 Oct 2026). Winslow writes on 4 Mar that the reply is one 'which I am at a loss to know from whence it came, further than it was sent from Washington, D.C., I rather suppose from the Navy Department', and asks that it be passed to them: the recipient could not decipher it, and no clear text or decode is filed on the reel. The outgoing cable's content is known in substance from the Philomel letter (a crib: wireless, 2000 metres, Honolulu, automatic working). known.py: no hits for 763.72/9366, 27107744, Winslow; not in catalogue.json or earlier nara_* triage. | A US Government cipher cable of 1918 that its own addressee could not read, filed with its context: a small test of US Navy/State cipher systems of the First World War, with a near-crib for the outgoing message. | 2 | 2 | 4 | B | ◇ |

Friedman wrote in 1948 that the Riverbank cipher records were thought destroyed after Fabyan's death (Cora Tyzzer letter, NSA A69876) and that the LoC Fabyan collection held none of them; the NYPL boxes came via Fabyan's widow to George Curtis (gift 1960), so these two boxes may be the only survivors. NSA historians (Dave Hatch and a colleague, a November visit, year not given) went through all nine Riverbank boxes and found them 'very duplicative and mixed': page proofs of Riverbank publications, student folders and exercises on graph paper, a few Parker Hitt letters; no cipher intercepts are mentioned (NSA blog 'A great TDY', Doc ID 6919113, released 30 Mar 2026). | The only known surviving working files of the first US government cryptanalytic unit (Riverbank 1917-18); any message they hold unread is WWI German-Mexican traffic. | 2 | 1 | 3 | B | ◇ |

## Read or resolved here, and removed

- **826 — British agent at Port Sainte-Marie → the Duke of Newcastle, c. July 1729 (Huntington mssBLA 191 p. 5)**: key recovered from adjacent plaintext, 28 Oct 2026. Code table rebuilt from the interlinear decipherments on the sibling letters mssBLA 187/188 and the 14 July, 29 June and later letters; 134 of 141 groups read. See targets/portstemarie1729/.
- **651 — Joel R. Poinsett → James Monroe, 14 June 1814 (NARA M37 roll 2 frames 0097-0100)**: read from existing decipherment, 28 Oct 2026. The clerk's interlinear decipherment is on the original (frame 0098) and Manning printed it in 1925 (vol. 1 doc. 201); both copies transcribed, 122 of 123 groups. Its code is the key of the 1813 Santiago letter (no. 639, still open); write-up poinsett1813.
- **653 — Powhatan Ellis → John Forsyth, Mexico City despatches of 1836 and No. 9 of 16 Nov 1839 (NARA M97 rolls 8–10)**: read from existing decipherment, 27 Oct 2026. Michael Brackx (issue #120) found the Department's decipherments filmed with every coded despatch but 26 Oct 1836, which Bosch García (1984) prints; WAINUT (PR #107) transcribed No. 9 and aligned it with its clear copy. The groups decode with the JQA table (`targets/jqa/code_table.tsv`); 14 disputed 1839 groups settled on the frames, and 26 Oct 1836 continues onto frame 0324 (three groups). Write-up `ellis1839`.
- **409 — Venceslau de Lima → King Manuel II, code telegrams of Nov-Dec 1909 (ANTT PT/TT/CAM/M09)**: read from existing decipherment, 27 Oct 2026 (WAINUT, PR #105). The receiver pencilled the decode above the groups; eight coded telegrams on the King's state visit to Spain, France and England and his return journey, 400 of 409 code items read; 261 values of a two-part code paired. See targets/lima1909/.
- **629 — Gen. Joseph E. Johnston → Secretary of War Seddon, Jackson, 16 Jun 1863 (NARA RG 109 naId 3854726)**: existing decipherment found, 27 Oct 2026. The War Department's "Translation of Cypher" is image 3 of the item; the text is printed in 1864 and in OR I 24 pt. 1 p. 227. The key MANCHESTERBLUFF fits when it advances by plaintext length (26/33); ISDX is ISLX. Contributed by WAINUT. See [`targets/johnston1863/`](targets/johnston1863/).
- **644 — Rose O'Neal Greenhow, letter in cipher on mourning paper, 1861 (NARA RG 59 naId 1634036)**: deciphered in part on 27 Oct 2026 with the key found on her body in 1864 (NARA M1091 naId 62017285 image 0484, not 0483). Side 1 about 60% of words as sense; side 2 and the figure scrap open. Contributed by WAINUT. See [`targets/greenhow1861/`](targets/greenhow1861/).
- **645 and 646 — Thomas Jordan → "My Dearest Rachel" (Greenhow), 1861 (NARA naId 1634051 images 1-2 and naId 6925618)**: one letter, resolved 27 Oct 2026. 646 is the cipher original (Jordan → Greenhow, not Greenhow → unknown); 645 images 1-2 are its clear copy; the 1864 Greenhow key fits the cipher unchanged. Contributed by WAINUT. See [`targets/jordan1861/`](targets/jordan1861/).
- **617 — De Puebla → Miguel Pérez de Almazán, London, 21 Apr 1506, AGS Patronato Real leg. 54 doc. 78 (PARES 2208120)**: read in part on 27 Oct 2026 with Tomokiyo's reconstruction of Puebla's First Cipher (contributed by WAINUT, PR #101); the cipher passages of ll. 18–29 read as sentences, ll. 11–17 and the clear text open. Shelfmark corrected: leg. 54 doc. 78, not "Patronato Real (not yet opened)". [write-up](https://dbourdeau.github.io/cyphersolver/puebla1506.html)
- **616 — Ferdinand and Isabella → De Puebla, Almazán, 21 Jun 1496, ciphered article, AGS Patronato Real leg. 52 doc. 47 f. 396**: resolved 27 Oct 2026 (WAINUT, PR #101). Deciphered at the time (the minuta carries the article in clear, note on f. 397v) and calendared by Bergenroth, CSP Spain I no. 138; the unit also holds the clear drafts nos. 137 and 141. A three-line sample decoded with the extant key PTR leg. 52 doc. 33; no page (targets/puebla1496/).
- **636 — Robert R. Livingston → John Jay, Philadelphia, 28 Nov 1781, "Make this addition to your cypher" (ALS NHi Jay Papers EJ 598)**: existing decipherment found, 27 Oct 2026. The line the Selected Papers of John Jay call undecipherable is glossed in Livingston's draft and entered on Jay's copy of the Thomson code: be, ce, de, fe, ge, he = 600-605 (226 = e, not r). See [`targets/livingston1781/`](targets/livingston1781/).
- **380 — João IV → the marquês de Nisa, ambassador in Paris, ANTT Manuscritos da Livraria 1017, letters 9, 13, 44, 49, 56, 153, 1642–44**: read in part on 27 Oct 2026, key recovered from adjacent plaintext. Alphabet A rebuilt from the letter-book's own clear copies (letters 8, 9, 13); alphabet B (Greek-shaped signs, 1644-45) from the volume's list of deciphered passages (m0276) against two 1645 siblings. 398 of 438 cipher words read; the 1643 runs illegible at 1060 px; five words of letter 153 open. Write-up: [joao1642](https://dbourdeau.github.io/cyphersolver/joao1642.html).
- **542 — Le Mercier de La Rivière and La Touche (Martinique) → the Navy minister (Berryer), ANOM COL C8 A 64 f° 1, 12 Jun 1761**: read in part on 27 Oct 2026, key recovered from adjacent plaintext. The two-part code was rebuilt from the interlinear decipherment of the sibling letter C8 A 63 f° 208 (21 Aug 1761) and extended from context; 754 of 818 groups read as sense (92.2%), about 40 single-use code words open. Write-up mercier1761.
- **484 — Jefferson-era legation codes Nos. 10, 13 and 16, residual groups (Short 26 Jul 1792, Carmichael 14 Apr 1788, Thomas Pinckney 28 Aug 1793), LoC Jefferson Papers ser. 1 and NARA M30 roll 2**: existing decipherment checked, 27 Oct 2026. 737 code groups transcribed, 720 with a reading (97.7%); the editors' readings confirmed from contemporary decodings in sibling letters; Pinckney's 'undeciphered 497' is 447; open: Short 401 ×2, 1083, 359 199 34 724, Pinckney 447, Carmichael 597, each a single occurrence. See [targets/legation1788/](targets/legation1788/). [Write-up](https://dbourdeau.github.io/cyphersolver/legation1788.html)
- **630 — Cornwallis ↔ Nisbet Balfour intercepted cipher letters, NARA RG 360, Papers of the Continental Congress item 51 vol. 1, pp. 717–736**: read from the existing decipherment on 27 Oct 2026. Balfour → Cornwallis, Nos. 1–3 and a second letter (March 1781), and Balfour → Stewart (12 Aug 1781), each with a 1781 interlinear decipherment; the Common cipher's ring and setting rule and the Stewart table rebuilt from it, all numbers deciphered again (99.8%). The Cornwallis → Wemyss/Balfour and Craig → Cornwallis passages have translations on pp. 759–761, not transcribed. [`targets/balfour1781/`](targets/balfour1781/) · [write-up](https://dbourdeau.github.io/cyphersolver/balfour1781.html)
- **631 — Papers of the Continental Congress, Miscellaneous Papers (PCC item 59 vol. 1), 'communications in cipher' filed with the keys of Franklin, Jay and Dumas**: closed, already deciphered, 27 Oct 2026. The seven cipher pieces are the office's own encipherment worksheets and attested copies with the English on the page, or are printed: Livingston → Franklin 26 Nov 1781 (worksheet pp. 325-328 + 169-172; Papers of Benjamin Franklin 36), Committee for Foreign Affairs → Jay 16 June 1780 (Jay Papers 2), Thomson's dictionary-code note of 19 May 1780 (decoded in Jay's hand, Columbia), and resolves of 10 Aug 1781, 22 Jan, 8 Feb and 7 Aug 1782 (Journals). One variant against the Franklin edition: the worksheet has "one Month's continuance" where the edition prints "one years". Notes only (targets/pcc1780/NOTES.md), no write-up.
- **618 — Rodrigo González de Puebla (London) → King Ferdinand, 15 Apr 1507, AGS Patronato Real, Tratados con Inglaterra leg. 5 ff. 31–32 (PARES 2208061, probably f. 31)**: already in print, 27 Oct 2026. Puebla wrote two letters that day: f. 31, wholly in cipher, was deciphered at the time by Almazán; f. 32 is a short clear duplicate with a few cipher words. Both are calendared in Bergenroth, CSP Spain I (1862) nos. 511–512, pp. 408–410 (the sweep's "no Puebla letter in April 1507" was wrong), and printed in full Spanish with the remaining cipher words deciphered in the 1868 Supplement, nos. 14–15, pp. 90–99. Images not seen (PARES 429). Entry 617's PARES id corrected to 2208120. Notes only (targets/puebla1507/NOTES.md), no write-up.
- **569 — Count Georg Ernst zu Erbach → Landgrave Ludwig VI of Hesse-Darmstadt, HStAD D 4 Nr. 248/3 (39 letters, 1654–1670)**: key recovered from adjacent plaintext on 27 Oct 2026. Only three 1666 letters carry cipher (images 003, 004, 006): number pairs giving line and letter of a rhymed German Lord's Prayer, rebuilt from a contemporary Latin outline filmed beside the long letter; all three deciphered (591 of 610 pairs as the key gives them). Not the Auflösungen in D 4 Nr. 239/1, which hold a 1640s Georg II table. [write-up](https://dbourdeau.github.io/cyphersolver/erbach1653.html)
- **418 — Antoni Augustyn Deboli → King Stanisław August, cipher despatches from St Petersburg, 1789, AGAD Zbiór Popielów 17**: deciphered at the time, 27 Oct 2026. The cabinet's Polish decipherments are the same-date texts in ZbPop 419 (103 of 106; 3 in ZbPop 417). The 6 Jan pair was aligned in the 1790 code (1559 = w, 951 = od, repeated 355 and 1567 at Hiszpańskiego/Hiszpanij and wyiednała/wypuszczenie). Then (27–28 Oct 2026, targets/deboli1789) eleven pairs aligned, the code rebuilt (630 groups) and the three despatches without a clear text read in part: 5,094 of 5,903 groups. Write-up deboli1789. [`targets/deboli1789/`](targets/deboli1789/) · [`targets/deboli1790/`](targets/deboli1790/)
- **420 — Antoni Augustyn Deboli → King Stanisław August, cipher despatches from St Petersburg, 1791, AGAD Zbiór Popielów 5**: deciphered at the time, 27 Oct 2026. The cabinet's Polish decipherments are the same-date texts in ZbPop 421 (98 of 105). The 7 Jan pair was aligned: "ani od WKMci, ani od" = 1944 951 1570 1944 951, as in 1790. Notes only. [`targets/deboli1790/`](targets/deboli1790/) Five despatches transcribed and aligned group by group with their decipherments (98.9% of 3,082 groups; two codes): [`targets/deboli1791/`](targets/deboli1791/) · [write-up](https://dbourdeau.github.io/cyphersolver/deboli1791.html)
- **264 (R1871 part) — Sebastiano Foscarini (Paris) to the Doge, despatch no. 117, 11 Sept 1680, ASVe Busta 30 f. 4 (DECODE R1871)**: read from existing decipherment, 27 Oct 2026; removed. Paolo Bonavoglia's decipherment (crittologia.eu/storia/SebFoscarini_Parigi16800911.html; original filza 171A, chancery decipherment filza 166) was offline during the attempt here (22 Sept 2026, ciphertext-only annealing failed) and is back online; Brice Dudout reported it and rebuilt the table (five-code syllabary blocks, out of order). [write-up](https://dbourdeau.github.io/cyphersolver/r1871.html), [targets/r1871/](targets/r1871/NOTES.md).
- **391 — Afonso VI (countersigned Castelo Melhor) to the conde de Vila Flor, ANTT Luís de Miranda Pereira liv. 2 (PT/TT/LMP/0002)**: read by Brice Dudout, 27 Oct 2026, not here; removed. The cipher letters are of May 1663, not 1660-61: four letters read at 97-99% (13, 15 and 26 May 1663 and a note of 15 May), key checked on a held-out letter, on duplicate copies and on a sentence clear in one copy and enciphered in the other; leaves m0057 and m0059 are swapped in the volume. Not in Ericeira. Europe chiffrée, documents.html#vilaflor-1663.
- **498 — Ragusa intelligence to Ferdinand I (Caraffa, Ferducci), HHStA Türkei I 1-5-12 to 2-2-24, 1530-32**: resolved, 27 Oct 2026 (Brice Dudout), not here; removed. Every piece but 2-2-19 has a contemporary gloss; Dudout read 2-2-19 (Ferducci, Fiume, 19 July 1532) with codes rebuilt from the glosses of 2-2-9 and 2-2-24, agreeing 6/6 with an independent 1542 table (catalogue 499). Ferducci offers to seize the French ambassador at sea, probably Antonio Rincon. Europe chiffrée, documents.html#ferducci-1532.
- **439 — Ludwik Wąsowicz → Aleksander Michał Lubomirski, ANK AKPot 3227 (DECODE R7501–R7511), 1662–63**: read by Brice Dudout, 27 Oct 2026, not here; removed. A simple substitution, one two-digit number per letter, read with the nineteenth-century table R7501 and checked blind on the letter of 5 May 1663 (R7508); seven letters of 1662–63, not 1662–69. R7510 is the end of the Jarosław letter of 9 Dec 1663 (not 1665) that begins in R7509; R7502 is already deciphered between the lines and on the sheet R7511. Read from DECODE images shared for study; none reproduced. Europe chiffrée, documents.html#krakow-1663.
- **626 — Lope Hurtado de Mendoza → Charles V, Tordesillas, 10 Dec 1520, AGS PTR leg. 2 doc. 36,8 (PARES 12988891)**: read by Brice Dudout, 27 Oct 2026, not here; removed. Wholly in cipher, sent the same day as the clear letter PTR leg. 2 doc. 36,6 that Danvila printed (MHE XXXVI pp. 688–690). Paz's slip points to a key in the letter of 23 Sept 1520 (36,2), which does not fit; Dudout rebuilt a homophonic letter substitution (about 35 signs, dotted sigla for persons) from the letter itself, checked it on held-out lines and read about 97.7% of some 920 cipher words. The sigla other than ·fre· (probably the Admiral) are unidentified. Europe chiffrée, documents.html#lope-hurtado-1520.
- **485 — Francis Dana → Robert R. Livingston, St Petersburg, 6/17 Apr 1783, PCC item 89 vol. II p. 730**: read independently by WAINUT and by Brice Dudout, 27 Oct 2026; removed. WAINUT recovered the three shifted alphabets from the ciphertext alone and read the eight lines in part, four code groups open ([`targets/dana1783/`](targets/dana1783/), in progress). Dudout broke it the same way, then found Dana's own table of October 1782 in the same volume (p. 656: alphabets from n, w and i, a nomenclator numbered 30–305), which reads all eight lines. Europe chiffrée, documents.html#dana-1783.
- **638 — Alexander H. Everett → Henry Clay, Madrid, 25 Sept 1825, "Notes of a conversation with Mr Zea", NARA M31 reel 27**: read independently by WAINUT and by Brice Dudout, 27 Oct 2026, both with the code table of targets/jqa; removed. Dudout read all of the cipher, pp. 1–6 included (74 + 1,127 groups, 0.986 of the second part), after checking the table on the despatch of 8 Sept 1825 against the Department's decoding (Manning doc. 1133): 288 of 304 groups agree. Europe chiffrée, documents.html#everett-1825.
- **652 — William H. Crawford → James Monroe, Paris, 15 Aug 1813 (not 3 Sept), NARA M34 roll 17 frames 0027–0029**: read independently by WAINUT and by Brice Dudout, 27 Oct 2026, both with the code table of targets/jqa; removed. WAINUT read 1,313 of 1,368 groups but dated the letter 3 Sept from the heading group 954 read as "3rd" ([`targets/crawford1813/`](targets/crawford1813/), in progress); Dudout read 1,330 of 1,371 groups and the heading 932 939 932 954 as the digits 1813. Europe chiffrée, documents.html#crawford-1813.
- **751 — Marmont → Jourdan, 1 June 1812, AHN Diversos-Colecciones 134 N.73**: read in part by Brice Dudout, 27 Oct 2026 (pull request #162, `targets/marmont1812/`); removed. The 1812 Grand Chiffre deciphering table (SHD "B n° 30", J.-F. Bouchaudy's photographs) applied unchanged; about 26 numbers unresolved (copying errors). With it, Jourdan → Soult, 28 May 1812 (N.34) read. [write-up](https://dbourdeau.github.io/cyphersolver/marmont1812.html)
- **724 — Colonel Jardet → Marshal Marmont, Paris, 6 March 1812, AHN Diversos-Colecciones 133 N.29**: resolved, 27 Oct 2026 (Brice Dudout, `targets/marmont1812/`); removed. The AHN piece is itself a decipherment of the time ("copia descifrada conforme"), with the Spanish reconstruction of the key attached: a homophonic cipher of 48 numbers on a line of Voltaire's Tancrède, not the Grand Chiffre of the other pieces.
- **419 — Antoni Augustyn Deboli → King Stanisław August, cipher despatches from St Petersburg, 1790, AGAD Zbiór Popielów 4**: deciphered at the time, 27 Oct 2026. All 109 despatches have the cabinet's Polish decipherment, filed apart: 2 Jan–2 Feb 1790 in ZbPop 417 k. 353–386, 5 Feb–31 Dec in ZbPop 420 (the "open despatches of the same day" of the entry). Paired by date and heading; code groups aligned on 2 Jan and 9 Feb (1559 = w, 1092 = po-, 606 = z). A Polish syllable-and-word code, not rebuilt. Notes only, no write-up. [`targets/deboli1790/`](targets/deboli1790/)
- **466 — Duke Frederik of Schleswig-Holstein ↔ Lübeck, 1523, Rigsarkivet Sønderjyske Fyrstearkiver, Hertug Frederik (1.), Sager vedrørende udlandet item 8 (Arkivalieronline epid 14908271, images 94–129)**: already in print, 26 Oct 2026. The "chifferskrift" is a name code: single signs for persons, places, days and troops in clear Low German. The key strip (Gemeinsch. Arch. cap. XIII, 38, endorsed by Wolf von Utenhof) is reproduced on the plate facing p. 312 of Schäfer and Techen, *Hanserecesse* III/8 (1910). That volume prints the coded letters (nn. 279–354) with every sign resolved; image 94 is its n. 292, witness K1 (XIII 47c). Key table in `targets/frederik1523/key.tsv`; notes only, no write-up.
- **483 — Jefferson's Code No. 11 (Barclay–Lamb code), Barclay, Carmichael, Short and Jefferson, 1786–1791, LoC Jefferson Papers ser. 1 and NARA M34 roll 2**: key recovered from adjacent plaintext on 27 Oct 2026, partial. 348 values rebuilt from Jefferson's interlinear decodings and clear-text sheets; 1,868 of 1,917 groups read; the editors' readings checked group by group ([sea] at 495 contradicted; Barclay's footnote = The Pro-cur-e-r [General?]). Mountflorence → Madison (addressed to Marshall), Paris, 18 March 1801, NARA RG 59 Consular Despatches Paris (T1 roll 1, frame 0097)**: key recovered from the ciphertext alone on 26 Oct 2026, a one-part alphabetical code broken from four spelled names; all 39 groups decoded (the Louisiana retrocession for Tuscany); one Founders figure corrected (251, not 250). `targets/mountflorence1801/`.

The Burgo letter cited by Galende 1994 p. 163 is not on the record and was not located. [Write-up](https://dbourdeau.github.io/cyphersolver/burgo1527.html), removed 28 Sept 2026.

G. von Ilten in the scan's list (Ms XXIII 1234:29,2) were deciphered with the code table in Ms XXIII 1234:31,1 (`targets/ilten1743/`).

Homophonic two-digit key (70 values) rebuilt here from context cribs; none of the Swedish keys on DECODE fits. 246 of 274 cipher tokens (89.8%) read: *nach der Oberpfaltz und gegen die [442]*, *die in Schlesien agirende [361]*, *mit guten Fürsichtigkeit nachvolgen*. - **287 — Isabella of Castile to the Duke of Estrada, 20 Aug 1503, AGS Estado, Tratados con Inglaterra leg. 4 ff. 65–67 (now Patronato Real leg. 53 doc. 69)**: read in part, 22 Sept 2026. The letter covers the French war on Roussillon and Fuenterrabía and asks Henry VII for 2,000 English foot, not the marriage. - **263 — Unknown sender (Roma) to unknown recipient, 29 Apr 1628, ASVe IT ASVe 0045 010 Busta 27 f. 354 (DECODE R1862)**: read in part, 22 Sept 2026. A Venetian ambassador's despatch to the Doge. Write-up docs/r1862.html
- **168 — Johann Arndt (1555-1621) (Glücksbrunn) to unknown recipient, 18 Sep 1798, Beinecke Mellon MS 136 (DECODE R2873)**: read, 22 Sept 2026. Its 31 cipher passages (pp. 24–76) are in a Rosicrucian pigpen alphabet whose key is drawn on p. 83; all read with it, 1,545 signs, 2 unread. Page 24 had been read online by Lasry and Kopal (Schmeh, Cipherbrain, March 2022). See [targets/mellon136/](targets/mellon136/).

- **163 — Cornelio Sperantio to ..., 2 ciphertexts, BayHStA Kurbayern Äußeres Archiv 4591 (DECODE R9411, R9412)**: read in part, 22 Sept 2026. - **122 — Unknown sender to ..., Feb 1572, BL Harley MS 260 f 419 (DECODE R8364)**: read in part, 22 Sept 2026. The six-sign place name reads VALERY (St Valery), the same word as in four letters printed by Digges and in R8363; a nine-sign run and three person codes stay open, the 1571 key (SP 106/2 f. 141A) and the original (Cotton Vespasian F VI) not being online. Norbert Biermann and Thomas Bosbach broke the key in March 2018; their keys and a decryption are filed as documents on DECODE R215 (only R215–R225 are marked "Partially decrypted"). Removed 21 Sept 2026. See [targets/pallotto1629/](targets/pallotto1629/).

- **237 — Monsignor Giovanni Battista Pallotto (Vienna) to Cardinal Barberini, 28 ciphered despatches, BAV Barb.lat. 6960, DECODE R286–R313 (4 Aug – 29 Nov 1629)**: the contents have been in print since 1897. Hans Kiewning, *Nuntiaturberichte aus Deutschland* IV/2, *Nuntiatur des Pallotto 1628–1630*, Bd. 2: *1629* (Berlin 1897) prints some forty of these despatches headed *dechiffr.*, from the copies deciphered in Rome (ASV Nunz. di Germania 119); the identification was confirmed against the register's own clear pages and its enclosure on p. 13. The cipher itself is not broken and no partial key is claimed (a held-out test rules the apparent one out); calibrated controls rule out every fixed-width hypothesis — a search of all 1,161,303 letters of the edition finds no window of four ciphertexts enciphering anything in print at width 2, 3 or 4 — and one positive finding identifies the system: 39 repeated 24-digit strings where chance gives none, which excludes real homophony — a code with deterministic variable-length groups. The sibling entry 236 (Barb.lat. 6956, Pallotto 1628, 70 ciphertexts) stays open, but Kiewning's Band 1 (1628) is the obvious place to look first. [Write-up](https://dbourdeau.github.io/cyphersolver/pallotto1629.html). **Update 21 Sept 2026:** George Lasry had found years ago that 6960 uses the same key as 6956 (Biermann and Bosbach, 2018, on DECODE R215); applied here, it reads all 28 ciphertexts apart from ~1,750 nomenclator groups missing from that key.

- **160 — Beatrice d'Aragona (1482–1505)**: four earlier printed readings and one plain letter, verified 20 Sept 2026. March editorial markers remain unexplained. Split by key on 14 Oct 2026: [1482](https://dbourdeau.github.io/cyphersolver/beatrice1482.html), [March 1486](https://dbourdeau.github.io/cyphersolver/beatrice1486.html), [May 1486](https://dbourdeau.github.io/cyphersolver/beatrice1486b.html), [1505, not a cipher](https://dbourdeau.github.io/cyphersolver/beatrice1505.html).

DECODE R4282 was separated from entry 207 on 14 Oct 2026 after George Lasry recovered its key with CTTS; see [the standalone write-up](https://dbourdeau.github.io/cyphersolver/decode4282.html). Entry 207 remains open for its other 11 records; its identifier is retained.

id 12, the Forget–Matignon–Mayenne leaves of BnF fr. 15572/15571, removed the same day and restored on 14 Oct 2026 narrowed to the unattempted Cipher-2 leaves ff. 218–219, its Cipher-1 and Cipher-3 leaves now the entries matignon1586 and matignon1586c3; id 9, BnF Espagnol 318, removed the same day and restored on 14 Oct 2026 narrowed to the unread nos. 93–94, its nos. 5, 92 and 95 now separate entries (federico1497, esp318, esp318no95); id 38, Carpio to Fuenmayor 1677, read and removed the same day; id 40, Balbases to Fuenmayor 1677–78, DECODE R985–R998, key rebuilt from the margins and all fourteen read (four never deciphered before), removed the same day; id 215, Frederick II to Michell 1751, found printed in the Politische Correspondenz and removed the same day; id 62, the TNA SP 106/10 worksheets R658–R702, shown to be the sp106box10 codebreaker's sheets (his grid rebuilds the Venetian three-figure code), removed 21 Sept 2026; id 56, the TNA SP 106/10 pigpen letter, DECODE R927, broken and read in part and removed the same day; id 243, Morosini to Montalto 1588–89, DECODE R18–R58, read with Meister's printed key and removed the same day (split on 14 Oct 2026: R53/R54, in a second key, are morosini1589, read in part with Lasry's partial key); ids 54, 55, 59 and 60, the Henrietta Maria circle letters of 1645–46 in TNA SP 106/10 ff. 207–247 (DECODE R752–R929), found already read by George Lasry, whose keys and plaintexts are on the DECODE records (2020), and removed the same day; see targets/hm1645/NOTES.md; id 67, Kurz von Senftenau to Trauttmansdorff 1639, DECODE R3811–R4736, key rebuilt from the R3811 glosses and all nine letters read in part, removed the same day; id 240, Acciaiuoli from Lisbon to the Secretariat 1758–60, DECODE R25, R195–R201, Lasry's letter stream read as Italian with 25 code words fixed from the leaves deciphered at the time, removed the same day). Their readings are in [SOLVED_CATALOGUE.md](SOLVED_CATALOGUE.md), on the site's [solved](https://dbourdeau.github.io/cyphersolver/solved.html) page and in the linked directories. Entry 7 now covers only the Ranzo letter to "Garbino" (fr. 3022 no. 20), the del Vasto items beside it being read; entries 7 and 20 were attempted here without a reading and stay in the open ranking. Id 216, Kauderbach's intercepted despatches from The Hague 1754–56 (KHA Prins Willem V inv. 201, DECODE R1043–R2082), unseparated figures split and the key found against the vocabulary of his 1761 key (DECODE R936), all ten read, removed the same day; see [targets/kauderbach1754/](targets/kauderbach1754/). Id 248, Barberini to Nuncio Ceva 1632 (AAV Segr. Stato Francia doss. 346, DECODE R75, R77, R78, R82, R84), found to be three-fifths already read by George Lasry, whose reconstructed key of 2020 is on every record of the dossier; the two letters he had not deciphered, R75 and R84, were read here and removed the same day; see [targets/ceva1632/](targets/ceva1632/). Id 249, the Secretariat's ciphered despatches to the nuncio in Spain 1718–20 (ASV Segr. Stato Spagna 364D, DECODE R154–R177), found already solved and read by George Lasry, whose reconstructed key and segmented decipherment of the whole Spagna 364 corpus are attached to every one of the 24 records (24 Oct 2020); measured at 97.6 % read, and 61 nomenclator groups his key left without a value recovered here from the alphabetical runs and the corpus contexts; removed on 20 Sept 2026; see [targets/nunzio1718/](targets/nunzio1718/). Id 57, the seven anonymous Italian ciphertexts of TNA SP 106/10 (DECODE R657, R660, R664, R704, R720–R722), shown to be one Jacobean codebreaker's working file, dated from its own nomenclature to 1623–24, its cipher explained from the key he wrote out (DECODE R725, catalogued as a key and so outside the entry) and its three-figure code rebuilt far enough to read phrases; removed on 20 Sept 2026; see [targets/sp106box10/](targets/sp106box10/). Id 17, Henri IV to Maisse at Venice 1592–93 (BnF fr. 16093 ff. 370, 373, 406, 410), read: two ciphers, not one, each with a key Tomokiyo had published as an image and never applied, and f. 370 verified letter-for-letter against a clear copy in Brienne 13; removed on 20 Sept 2026; see [targets/maisse1592/](targets/maisse1592/). Id 19, the Spanish despatches of 1593 (BnF fr. 3983 nos. 45, 79 and fr. 3984 nos. 47, 68), read in part: the Spanish office's own key, with its nomenclature, found at BnF fr. 3995 f. 97 through the DECODE key records 4076-4077, and Tomokiyo's two key images confirmed against it; removed on 20 Sept 2026; see [targets/sessa1593/](targets/sessa1593/) (no. 68, in the Feria–Mansfeld cipher, split off on 14 Oct 2026 to [targets/ibarra1593/](targets/ibarra1593/)). ## Also noted, not counted

<!-- also:start -->
- **Riksarkivet key-box and Oxenstierna ciphers, 8 records (Bremen 1631, R4282, R4306 and Rusdorff 1625 read or partly read and removed)**, 1628 – 1633, Riksarkivet, TNA of Sweden (8 items), [DECODE R4284](https://de-crypt.org/decrypt-web/RecordsView/4284), [DECODE R4333](https://de-crypt.org/decrypt-web/RecordsView/4333), [DECODE R4334](https://de-crypt.org/decrypt-web/RecordsView/4334), +5 more records. DECODE R4284–R4341, 8 records in four different ciphers, each its own entry since the one-key split of 14 Oct 2026. Viewed 21 Sept 2026. The two Bremen letters of 1631 (R4330–R4331, riksarkivet1628.html) are read and removed from this entry; R4282 was deciphered by George Lasry (decode4282.html). R4306: contributed partial Dutch decipherment by George Lasry, transcribed with CTTS then solved with Opus 5.5 (17 Oct 2026; sweden4306.html, which also records this project's failed attempt of 21 Sept 2026); pencilled 1632? and Amsterdam attribution remain qualified, four code identities open. R4336–R4337 turned out to be Rusdorff's London letters of February 1625 in a homophonic cipher with an alphabetical nomenclator; key recovered from the ciphertext by George Lasry (21 Oct 2026, PR #72; rusdorff1625.html) and removed from this entry. Open: R4284 (Latin 1628, Camerarius docket; riksarkivet4284.html) — attacked with Latin annealing and against two box keys, not broken; R4333–R4335 (Rusdorff → Oxenstierna 1628, another cipher; rusdorff1628.html) and R4338–R4341 (E 708, Swedish, June 1633, not 1646; glossed in part at the time; oxenstierna1633.html) surveyed only. One remaining key-box ciphertext that resisted a first attack, and Oxenstierna correspondence of 1628 and 1633 with a key collection that may hold their keys. Imp. 3, solv. 4, diff. 3, class A, priority 5.9.
- **Paris 1719 code letters, 2 ciphertexts**, 7 and 10 Feb 1719, BL, Add MS 32305 ff. 6–7 (2 items), [DECODE R2964](https://de-crypt.org/decrypt-web/RecordsView/2964), [DECODE R2965](https://de-crypt.org/decrypt-web/RecordsView/2965). Viewed 21 Sept 2026 (targets/bl32305/). R2963 and R2974 were deciphered at the time and are dropped. R2964/R2965 (Paris 7 and 10 Feb 1719): two-part 3-figure code, ~12 contemporary glosses, 354 groups in f. 6. The Carré letters R2968/R2970/R2972 (a different code) were split off on 14 Oct 2026 to item 70 (targets/carre1742/). Ciphered letters from Paris to a correspondent in England, February 1719; what the code hides is not known. Imp. 3, solv. 3, diff. 3, class B, priority 5.0.
- **Throckmorton leaf 1559: marginal word-sign code, and John Wood to Cecil 1568**, 10 Jul 1559 – 8 Aug 1559, BL, Add MS 4136 (2 items), [DECODE R2988](https://de-crypt.org/decrypt-web/RecordsView/2988), [DECODE R2989](https://de-crypt.org/decrypt-web/RecordsView/2989). Attempted 21 Sept 2026; split 14 Oct 2026 into one entry per cipher. Throckmorton's 10 July 1559 letter on f. 32 (Cipher 1) was deciphered in part in targets/throck1559/; since 23 Oct 2026 (Reading audit 22-23 Oct 2026 (George Lasry's test: a reading must build sentences)) it is decoded, not read, and open again. Still unread: the f. 32 margin (targets/throck1559margin/), a word-sign code (222 groups, 113 used once), probably a copy of the 8 July 1559 despatches; needs its key or TNA SP 70/5 (CSP For. i 947, 950). Wood's 39-sign line (6 Sept 1568, targets/wod1568/) has no unique solution ciphertext-only; needs Hatfield, Cecil Papers vol. 1. Ciphered despatches of Unknown sender to unknown recipient, 10 Jul 1559 – 8 Aug 1559; what the cipher hides is not known. Imp. 2, solv. 4, diff. 3, class A, priority 4.9.
- **English royalist letter in numerical code, September 1645 (SP 106/10 f. 251)**, Sept 1645, TNA, State Papers, inv.nr. 106 box 10, f. 251 · DECODE R931, [DECODE R931](https://de-crypt.org/decrypt-web/RecordsView/931). Attempted, open (21 Sept 2026; own entry sp106r931 since 14 Oct 2026). Of the four DECODE records first grouped here, R722 is the 1625 Venetian letter of the SP 106/10 codebreaker's file (now sp106r722, catalogue 66) and R656 and R662 are that codebreaker's worksheet and memorandum on it. Left here: R931, a strip of ~190 numbers 10-260 with clear words ('(1) septembre 1645', 'earnestly', 'reasons'), 104 distinct numbers: a nomenclator. Lasry's 1645-46 SP 106 keys, the R932 Goring key and the Charles I-Culpeper 1645 key (R9117/R9118) do not fit. A royalist despatch of autumn 1645, after Naseby; what it says is not known. Imp. 2, solv. 3, diff. 3, class B, priority 4.0.
- **Walsingham letter-book, Nov 1572 (Burghley, Leicester, Walsingham): name codes**, Nov 1572, BL, Harley MS 260 f 367, [DECODE R8361](https://de-crypt.org/decrypt-web/RecordsView/8361), [write-up](https://dbourdeau.github.io/cyphersolver/r8361.html). DECODE R8361: letter-book copies of four clear letters printed in Digges 1655 pp. 297-301; cipher is 8 boxed name codes and a nine-sign letter run. [3] = the Queen by context; [7], [9], H and the run unread, no key known. Ciphered letter of Unknown sender to unknown recipient, Nov 1572; what the cipher hides is not known. Imp. 2, solv. 3, diff. 4, class C, priority 3.4.
- **... to unknown recipient**, undated, BL, Add MS 32280 f 1-2, [DECODE R8870](https://de-crypt.org/decrypt-web/RecordsView/8870). DECODE R8870, viewed 21 Sept 2026: 901 numeric code groups (1-1647, hyphenated syllable compounds), ending 'Duplicata'; no decipherment on the leaves. None of the 27 key records of Add MS 32280 fits (R8890 French 6001+, R8894-R8919 Dutch 1823-42). Too little text for a ciphertext-only rebuild of a ~1,650-group code. Notes and transcription in targets/r8870/. Ciphered letter of ... to unknown recipient; what the cipher hides is not known. Imp. 2, solv. 2, diff. 3, class B, priority 3.1.
- **Unknown sender to unknown recipient**, 4 Aug 1728 (docket), BL, Add MS 32287 f 37-40, [DECODE R7707](https://de-crypt.org/decrypt-web/RecordsView/7707). DECODE R7707 viewed 22 Sept 2026: f. 37r = 205 invented cursive signs; ff. 38-40 = a contemporary codebreaker's tallies, contact tables and guesses (no reading), a household bill, docket 4 Aout 1728 / 31 Aout / 5 8bre. IoC 1.07, not a simple substitution; mono, periodic and Quagmire-type anneals failed. Needs the key or the sibling letters. Ciphered letter of Unknown sender to unknown recipient; what the cipher hides is not known. Imp. 1, solv. 3, diff. 3, class B, priority 3.0.
- **Bavarian key volume: letter to Duke Wilhelm V (1583), unread**, 1583, BayHStA, Kurbayern Äußeres Archiv 4591 f. 274–277, [DECODE R9367](https://de-crypt.org/decrypt-web/RecordsView/9367), [write-up R9367](r9367.html). Of the 14 DECODE records in this entry, 12 were read or broken here (21 Sept 2026; split by key 15 Oct 2026 into kaa4591, kaa4591b, fulda1576, r9367 and r9416). Left open, each with its own page: R9424 (r9424), 12 June 1583 to Wilhelm V (Cologne war), monoalphabetic by IoC but no key found (R9422 cut off). R9291 is a key fragment. 23 Oct 2026, Reading audit 22-23 Oct 2026 (George Lasry's test: a reading must build sentences): R9367 (r9367, known key) is decoded, not read and is open again. 22 Oct 2026: R9319 (r9319, the 'Post Scripta' dot cipher of Ernst of Bavaria, 1583) was found deciphered in full by A. C. Leighton, ZBLG 37 (1974) 828-844 (issue #88, ry-xu), and taken out of this entry. 23 Oct 2026: R9424 (r9424) key recovered ciphertext-only by Ryan Xu (issue #89) and read in part here on the images (92.8% of words); taken out of this entry, which now covers R9367 only. Ciphered despatches of Unknown sender to unknown recipient; what the cipher hides is not known. Imp. 1, solv. 3, diff. 3, class B, priority 3.0.
- **A Venetian secretary to the Venetian ambassador in England, 1625, in a three-figure syllabic code (SP 106/10 ff. 193-195)**, first half of 1625, TNA, State Papers, inv.nr. 106 box 10, ff. 193-195 · DECODE R722, with the codebreaker's worksheets R703 (ff. 184-185), R656, R661, R662, R663, R667, R684, R701, R702, R720, [DECODE R722](https://de-crypt.org/decrypt-web/RecordsView/722), [DECODE R703](https://de-crypt.org/decrypt-web/RecordsView/703). Attempted, open (21 Sept 2026; restored 14 Oct 2026 for sp106r722). This entry first held only R703, closed on 21 Sept 2026 as a codebreaker's worksheet on a 'lost' 46-line letter; the letter is R722 (endorsed 'Cypher of a Venetian Secretary to the Embassador of that nation', 1625; Spinola before Breda, the Pope and Bethune in the clear passages). All 420 code groups (117 types) transcribed; the codebreaker's partial key on R701 p. 3 and clear-text junctions fix a few values; annealing does not converge. Split from sp106box10 under the one-key rule. A Venetian diplomatic letter of 1625 with the English codebreaker's failed attack on it; the code text is unread. Imp. 2, solv. 2, diff. 4, class B, priority 2.5.
- **Farnese chancery cipher, Spagna 1A (IA-1, DECODE R91), companion of Vatican Challenge Part 5**, Dec 1541 (letter on the Nuremberg diet and Buda), AAV, Segr. Stato, Spagna 1A (IA-1; DECODE R91), [DECODE R91](https://de-crypt.org/decrypt-web/RecordsView/91), [DECODE R92](https://de-crypt.org/decrypt-web/RecordsView/92). DECODE R91: five cipher page images and four cleartext Farnese letters of summer 1542, downloaded and measured here 18 Sept 2026 (targets/vatican5/NOTES.md). 2,956 digits; a different key and design from IA-2: doubled digits at 0.88 of chance (IA-2 0.30), wide gaps not word division. No key sheet, no decipherment on the record. The companion IA-2 (DECODE R92, the Farnese letter of 15 Apr 1542, Vatican Challenge Part 5) was solved by Simon Klee in Sept 2026 (targets/vatican5/SOLUTION.md) and is recorded in SOLVED_CATALOGUE.md; his key does not transfer. Farnese's ciphered despatch to the nuncio in Spain, December 1541, on the Nuremberg diet and Buda; unread. Imp. 1, solv. 3, diff. 4, class C, priority 2.4.

DECODE R1854 image 1 (the record holds four letters in four ciphers; images 2-5 deciphered here, now the entries r1854, mutiliana1428 and cattanei1430; this item is targets/malatesta1428/, split 14 Oct 2026). Three cipher runs, 262 letter-like signs (ſſ, η, ʒ, H, cc, ∩, I, ƀʒ ...) inside a clear Latin letter on the peace of Ferrara (April 1428). Not a simple or homophonic substitution in Latin or Italian (controls pass); the R1853 register's Malatesta keys do not fit. Pandolfo Malatesta's secret plans for his brother-in-law after the peace of Ferrara; one of the oldest unread cipher passages with images online. Imp. 1, solv. 2, diff. 3, class B, priority 2.1.
- **Letters to Mr Carré, Pall Mall, 1742–45, 3 ciphertexts**, Mar 1742 – 19 Jan 1745, BL, Add MS 32305 ff. 11–12, 14–17, 22–23 (3 items), [DECODE R2968](https://de-crypt.org/decrypt-web/RecordsView/2968), [DECODE R2970](https://de-crypt.org/decrypt-web/RecordsView/2970), [DECODE R2972](https://de-crypt.org/decrypt-web/RecordsView/2972). Viewed 21 Sept 2026 (targets/carre1742/, split on 14 Oct 2026 from bl32305, where it had been folded into item 78). R2968/R2970/R2972 (letters to Mr Carré, Pall Mall, Mar 1742, received 22 Aug 1742, 19 Jan 1745): transcribed in full (1323 groups, 381 distinct, 1–800); not a letter cipher (anneal = shuffled control), not one-part (r = −0.26): two-part code of ~800 entries, closed; R2969 is a frequency count, not a key. Three anonymous letters to a Mr Carré in Pall Mall, intercepted 1742–45, entirely in a code with no gloss; what they hide is not known. Imp. 2, solv. 1, diff. 4, class B, priority 1.6.
- **Trigram code fragment 'Suite du No 13 / No 24'**, undated, BL, Add MS 32280 f 3, [DECODE R8871](https://de-crypt.org/decrypt-web/RecordsView/8871). DECODE R8871, viewed 21 Sept 2026. The leaf is a ruled form in a French hand, 'Suite du No 13' / 'No 24', with 77 three-character groups (letters, digits, œ), 76 of them distinct and near-flat statistics. It is a large or enciphered code, too short to rebuild. None of the 26 DECODE key records of Add MS 32280 (R8890, R8894–R8919, 1790–1842, mostly Dutch numeric codes) fits. R8870 (ff. 1–2) is an unrelated numeric letter. Notes in targets/r8871/NOTES.md. An unidentified numbered trigram-code series copied by the Deciphering Branch; only No 24's tail is imaged. Imp. 1, solv. 1, diff. 3, class B, priority 1.2.
- **Intercepted letter from Brussels with three short number runs**, 3 Apr 1660 NS, Bodleian, MS Rawlinson A 67 (Thurloe papers vol. lxvii), p. 270; printed Thurloe State Papers vii 869, [source](https://www.british-history.ac.uk/thurloe-papers/vol7/pp860-869), [Cryptiana](https://cryptiana.web.fc2.com/code/thurloe.htm), [Cryptoole XXXXXX-1](https://cryptoole.satoru.net/case.html?id=XXXXXX-1). Cryptoole XXXXXX-1 (open). About 21 numbers in three runs (6, 10 and 5 figures, values 4-72), e.g. '61 50 57 62 72 66 54 61 68 60'; printed without decipherment. Reviewed 20 Oct 2026: all 21 numbers extracted from Birch VII p. 869 and screened against twelve existing transcribed key tables (research/catalogue_review_20261020/brussels_key_screen.json). No coherent reading identified; some tables are partial, so their families are not excluded. A royalist note from Brussels in the weeks before the Restoration; small but cheap to test. Imp. 1, solv. 1, diff. 3, class C, priority 1.2.

## Method

- Harvest: Gallica SRU `dc.description all "chiffre" and dc.type all "manuscrit"` → `research/gallica_sweep/sru_chiffre_desc.json`;
  items split on Omont's numbering and kept when they say *chiffre* without *déchiffrement*
  (`research/gallica_sweep/bnf_candidates.txt`). Shelfmarks resolved from IIIF manifests (`research/gallica_sweep/ark_shelfmarks.json`).
- Coverage: string search of correspondents against cryptiana `unsolved.htm` and the six French article pages saved
  in `research/gallica_sweep/src/`.
- DECODE refill: `research/catalogue_harvest/decode/dump_list.py` (record list), `dump_views*.py` (full records),
  `digest.py` (groups + same-series keys), `rule_score.py` (scores, merges, exclusions from `overrides.json`),
  `merge.py` (into `catalogue.json`). Cookie in `targets/bordeaux/decode/cookie.txt`, JWT from any RecordsView page.
- Not done: image inspection of ◇ entries; Tomokiyo's François I article; Scheurer, Savasse, Mousset editions;
  DECODE search for each item.

**Checked:** catalogue descriptions and item numbering; shelfmarks from the IIIF manifests; presence/absence of a *déchiffrement* item in the same
volume; fr. 3484 f. 34 on the image (cipher, no decipherment on the leaf); Tomokiyo's status wording for entries 11–14, 16–17, 19–21, 23–24; fr. 16127 on the image.
**Not checked:** the leaves of ◇ entries; printed editions that may contain clear texts; DECODE records.
**User must verify** before attacking any entry: open the ark at the item's folio and confirm no decipherment
follows, then search DECODE and Tomokiyo's site for the correspondent and date.


Removed 20 Sept 2026: **88, Nicholas Throckmorton, twenty Add MS 4136 records** — archived key and prior printed counterparts verified on two samples; see [result](targets/throckmorton/RESULT.md). Full token alignment and composite-record non-Throckmorton material are not claimed solved.
